bib.title: AlpacaFarm: A Simulation Framework for Methods that Learn from Human Feedback

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AlpacaFarm: A Simulation Framework for Methods that Learn from Human Feedback". Yann Dubois, Xuechen Li, Rohan Taori, Tianyi Zhang (equal contribution), Ishaan Gulrajani, Jimmy Ba, Carlos Guestrin, Percy Liang, Tatsunori B. Hashimoto. The PDF is arXiv 2305.14387v4, dated 8 Jan 2024. The extracted text never names NeurIPS, so the venue comes from the caller, not the PDF. Year 2023.

COVERAGE: I read all 105,304 of 105,304 chars across 31 pages: main text, limitations, Appendices A–F, Tables 2–7, and the annotation guideline and interface. I skimmed the references for origins.

CLAIMS (ranked for the LLM-as-judge section)
- claim: Method rankings from the simulated judge pool match rankings from training and judging with humans.
  number: Spearman 0.98 (0.94 and R² 0.83 when the 5 API models the authors did not train are excluded)
  setup: 11 systems (6 LPF methods on LLaMA 7B plus GPT-4, ChatGPT, Davinci001, LLaMA 7B, Alpaca 7B). Win-rate vs Davinci003 on 805 eval instructions. Simulated methods were trained on p_ann_sim and judged by p_eval_sim. Human methods were trained on human prefs and judged by humans.
  quote: "the rankings have a Spearman correlation of 0.98, which suggests that AlpacaFarm faithfully captures the rankings among different LPF methods" / "Without those points, we have R2 = 0.83 and a Spearman Correlation of 0.94."
  where: p7 §4.2; Fig 3 caption p6
- claim: The pool of 13 simulated judges agrees with the human majority about as well as a held-out human does, at a fraction of the cost.
  number: 65% vs 66%; 25x cheaper ($300 → $12 per 1000)
  setup: Agreement with the majority vote of 3 crowdworkers on pairwise preferences over AlpacaFarm outputs
  quote: "our evaluator pevalsim (green) has a 65% agreement rate with the human majority vote, which is similar to the held-out human agreement rate at 66% (blue). At the same time, pevalsim is 25× cheaper ($300 → $12 per 1000 examples)."
  where: p7 §4.3
- claim: A single GPT-4 prompt can beat the pool on agreement, but the authors reject it because it lacks human-like variability.
  number: 68%
  setup: The best single GPT-4 prompt among the candidates in Fig 4
  quote: "one of the GPT-4 prompts achieving 68% agreement. While this high agreement level is impressive, we do not use single prompts directly for AlpacaFarm, as single prompts do not replicate the inter-annotator variability important for a simulator."
  where: p8
- claim: A low-variance single judge gives qualitatively wrong conclusions when used to train. With it, reward over-optimization disappears and best-of-1024 looks much better than PPO, which contradicts the human data.
  number: none
  setup: PPO, best-of-n and expert iteration with reward models trained on human, AlpacaFarm, and single-prompt GPT-4 (temperature 0) preferences
  quote: "simple GPT-4 feedback shows no overoptimization, leading to the false conclusion that the LPF methods can be optimized for much longer than is actually the case. For example, Figure 5 right shows best-of-1024 to be much better than PPO, which strongly disagrees with the results on human data."
  where: p8 §4.3
- claim: Annotator variance: the AlpacaFarm pools sit close to humans, and single GPT-4 sits far below them.
  number: 0.26 (eval pool), 0.43 (train pool), 0.35 (human), 0.1 (GPT-4)
  setup: Variance is the average error of a held-out annotation against the majority vote over 3 random draws
  quote: "At 0.26 for pevalsim and 0.43 for pannsim, AlpacaFarm is close to the human variance of 0.35; in contrast, the GPT-4 annotator has a much lower variance at 0.1."
  where: p8
- claim: Injected label noise is what drives over-optimization. Training labels are flipped 25% of the time, and 25% was the smallest flip rate tested that induced over-optimization.
  number: 25% flips; tested 0, 17(.5)%, 25%, 35%
  setup: Ablation with best-of-n over reward models trained on GPT-4, GPT-4 plus flips, the eval pool, and the eval pool plus flips
  quote: "we emulate intra-annotator variability by flipping the simulated preference 25% of the time, i.e., we inject random noise." / "added label noise provides the majority of the overoptimization effect" / "The exact ratio of 25% label noise was chosen to be the smallest considered ratio that induced overoptimization out of the ones we considered (0,17%,25%,35%)"
  where: p4 §3.2; p26 App E.1
- claim: Noise is used only during training. It is left out of evaluation because uniform noise does not change model rankings.
  number: none
  setup: Construction of the p_eval_sim judge
  quote: "We use the 13 simulated annotators described in Section 3.2 without injecting the additional noise (as adding uniform noise does not change model rankings)"
  where: p5 §3.3
- claim: Simulated judges share the human biases toward long answers and lists.
  number: length: humans 62%, sim 64%; lists: humans 69%, sim 63%
  setup: Pairwise preference rates
  quote: "humans prefer longer outputs 62% of the time, while our simulated annotators prefer those 64% of the time. Similarly, humans prefer outputs with lists 69% of the time, while our simulated annotators prefer those 63% of the time."
  where: p21 App C.2
- claim: Simulated judges also have biases humans do not: they favour the output shown first and outputs from their own model. The authors randomized order to control for this.
  number: none
  setup: Limitations section and App C.1
  quote: "we found that simulated annotators prefer the first outputs shown in the prompt and outputs that come from the same model as the simulator." / "We found randomization to be important given that the first output is often preferred by simulated annotators."
  where: p12 §7; p20 App C.1
- claim: Bias (error vs the human majority) is low for the pools and on par with the best GPT-4 judge. Single evaluators have less variance than humans.
  number: bias 0.38 (eval), 0.35 (train), 0.33 (GPT-4); single-evaluator variance <0.2 vs human 0.34
  setup: Fig 7. Bias is the majority of 4 simulated annotators vs the majority of 4 humans.
  quote: "single evaluators have a smaller variance (less than 0.2) than humans (blue line, 0.34)" / "both have low bias values (0.38 and 0.35) on par with one of our best GPT-4 annotators (0.33)."
  where: p21. Note: this gives human variance as 0.34, while the same paragraph and §4.3 give 0.35.
- claim: Most disagreement inside the judge pool comes from the underlying model, not from the prompt.
  number: none
  setup: Fig 8 pairwise-agreement heatmap; the pool has 5 GPT-4, 4 ChatGPT and 4 Davinci003 judges
  quote: "the largest source of variability between annotators comes from the underlying model, as illustrated by the clusters that arise from GPT4, ChatGPT and Davinci003 annotators."
  where: p21
- claim: Win-rates on the composite eval set track win-rates on real Alpaca Demo instructions.
  number: R² 0.97, Spearman 0.90
  setup: 11 systems judged by p_eval_sim on 200 filtered demo instructions vs the 805-instruction set
  quote: "R2 = 0.97 Spearman Correlation: 0.90"
  where: p9 Fig 6
- claim: There were two rank flips between simulated and human judging.
  number: SFT10k vs SFT52k human 44.3 vs 40.7, sim 36.7 vs 39.2; PPO vs ChatGPT human 55.1 vs 52.9, sim 46.8 vs 61.4
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "human annotators preferred SFT10k (44.3% vs 40.7%) while the simulator had the opposite preference (36.7% vs 39.2%, Table 2)"
  where: p7
- claim: The cost headline varies by passage: 50x, 45x and 25x. The overall experiment is $70 vs $3,150.
  number: $6 per 1000 (train annotator, 50x); 45x; Fig 1: $70/hours vs $3,150/days
  setup: The train annotator labels only half the outputs because of the Bernoulli mixture
  quote: "annotating 1000 outputs using simulated preference only costs $6, which is 50x cheaper than human annotation" / "at a cost that is 45x cheaper than crowdworkers"
  where: p4–5; p1
- claim: The human baseline was a qualified MTurk pool.
  number: 16 of 34 kept (>70% agreement with the authors); $21/hr median; $3000 for PREF; $242 per model eval
  quote: "we selected the 16 whose agreement rate was higher than 70% with the authors' annotations... a one-time $3000 cost of annotating our PREF split and a recurring $242 cost for evaluating a single model on the 805 evaluation instructions."
  where: p7 §4.1
- claim: There is a faithfulness-performance tradeoff. A noisy, faithful simulator is good for choosing a method, but a consistent single judge trains a better model for direct deployment.
  number: PPO on GPT-4 judge 50% vs PPO on AlpacaFarm 43% (human win-rate); PPO human 55%
  quote: "more faithful simulators, which display greater over-optimization, train objectively worse models."
  where: p11 Table 4

LIMITS: The tasks are simple and single-turn, and every fine-tuned model starts from LLaMA 7B. Human validation rests on a small crowd pool: §7 says "13 crowdworkers", while §4.1 says 16 were selected and App D says one outlier was removed. The crowd itself prefers long outputs. The method assumes an oracle LLM stronger than the models being trained. Hyperparameters do not transfer: the KL coefficient was 0.02 for human PPO and 0.002 for simulated PPO. There may be other judge biases the authors did not find. Pairwise win-rate "does not provide a deep understanding of the differences between two models". ChatGPT and GPT-4 were length-capped, which skews their win-rates. Length gains may hide hallucination. The judges are 2023 models (GPT-4-0314, ChatGPT, Davinci003), and the authors point to AlpacaEval for better automatic annotators.

BUILDS ON: The paper credits Chiang & Lee 2023 and G-Eval (Liu et al. 2023) for using LLMs as annotator proxies. It also cites Peng et al. 2023, Perez et al. 2022, and Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena). Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022) is the contrast case, because it adds no noise. Gao, Schulman & Hilton 2022 is cited for over-optimization. Methods: InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022), PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), Christiano et al. 2017, DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023), Quark (Lu et al. 2022), Bradley & Terry 1952, Stiennon et al. 2020 for best-of-n, and the Alpaca data (Taori et al. 2023). It also cites AlpacaEval (Li et al. 2023).

CODE: No code listings. The prompts are only at github.com/tatsu-lab/alpaca_farm. Practical judge tricks from App C.1 (p20):
- Randomize the order of the two outputs.
- Batch up to 5 items per GPT-4 call ("could fit batch size up to 20 ... without significantly decreasing performance").
- For ChatGPT, apply a negative logit bias to "Neither" and "Both", or ask for JSON with a short explanation and a boolean.
- Sample judges at temperature 1.0. The single GPT-4 judge uses temperature 0.

FIGURES:
- Fig 4 (p7), price vs human-mode agreement for every judge. It shows the cost and agreement claim in one picture.
- Fig 3 (p6), sim vs human win-rate scatter. It is the ranking-agreement claim in one picture.
- Fig 5 (p8), over-optimization appears for human and AlpacaFarm judges and not for single GPT-4. It shows why a deterministic judge misleads.
- Fig 7 (p21), bias vs variance of the judges.
- Fig 12/13 (p26), the label-noise ablation and flip-rate sweep.

PROBLEMS: There are no embedded instructions. The extraction is clean apart from figure-axis debris and split numbers in Table 2 ("69 .8"). Fig 4's caption refers to a colour symbol that did not extract. The figure data and the Fig 13 curves are images, so I read only their captions. The paper is internally inconsistent on the cost multiple (45x, 50x, 25x), on human variance (0.34 vs 0.35) and on the crowdworker count (13 vs 16).
